That is how the document is identified in e-court and it is a document has been produced through us through the Croatian state archives as are most of the other documents in this case. Concerning authenticity there is nothing about the document that has been produced that is any different than other document produced either by the Prosecution or the Defence in this case and I would submit there is no reason not to admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi some of your concerns seem to have been dealt with. Contemporaneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But it is a big difference between a document that was compiled and the witness statement. I don't know under which circumstances what the MUP had in mind within a week or weeks after -- after the events of getting information out of this gentleman. I just see it is a huge difference between the witness statement. We don't see the cover page, we don't see who the persons from the MUP who were present eliciting that information. For me it's a big difference between this statement and the normal document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will provide the entire document to the Prosecution. I will say that given that the Prosecution first let me say that given the Prosecution has admitted UNCIVPOL witness statements and other similar-type witness statements was taken by a different entity contemporaneously I don't see the objection as being well founded. Secondly these are all issues that go to weight and not to admissibility of the document anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think each of these CIVPOL documents were accompanied by people, witnesses who could talk about the procedures under which these documents were taken. I'm looking forward to the Defence case to see MUP officials from the Croatian authorities to talk about these witness statements and then they can be introduced at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether in every respect an accurate description of the documents that were tendered by the Prosecution is still to be seen. If I think about, for example, I think it was P320 attachments to -- a matter which has not been settled yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we do the following: Some of the concerns may be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I just make one point, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would draw Mr. Waespi's attention to Witness 136, I believe was her number, the first witness in this case where Mr. Waespi tendered witness statements because she was the translator. Mr. Flynn, who wasn't present for many of these HRAT witness statements they were tendered through Mr. Flynn several such witness statements where just because they were HRAT documents they were tendered he wasn't even present for the witness interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest the following at this moment. Apparently one of the things that is it bothering Mr. Waespi is that he doesn't have the -- the whole of the document, therefore I suggest that you provide Mr. Waespi with the documents in its entirety and then perhaps also discuss with him whether the whole of the document or just these portions you would like to tender whether there is in objections to see to what extent you a can agree on the matter. For the time being, I think you have read the whole portion of this document, which is relevant for the question you want to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's part of the record. Therefore, at this moment, I'll not invite Mr. Registrar to -- to assign a number to it. Leave it until you've spoken and then there's still an opportunity for you to re-tendered it and we know whether it is just this portion, whether there would be any further -- I'm looking at your expression Mr. Misetic. It is my suggestion surprises you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm only concerned that I forget about it later on that's why I told my case manager not to forget to come back to the issue. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is imaginable. Another way of dealing with the matter is that we assign a number to it at this moment. That we leave it marked for identification and we hear later from you and then at least it on the MFI list which is an advantage and a disadvantage because it is one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the document as it is -- at this moment present by Mr. Misetic would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D725 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it keeps that status until the parties have come back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkovic, I showed you several documents there. First you saw the note about the check-point being set up in Polace where UNCRO allegedly could not pass. Does that refresh your recollection about a check-point having been set up on the road from the direction of Knin towards Vrlika by the RSK army?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It doesn't, because there was no check-point. I saw UNPROFOR vehicles drive through Polace every day. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You also saw a document that says in -- after the signing of the Zagreb agreement in 1994 heavy weapons were withdrawn to the village of Polace. You are obviously familiar with Polace. Can you tell us where heavy weapons in the village of Polace may have been stored?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember there being any heavy weapons at all in 1994 and 1995. But perhaps the Polace that you have in mind is the one near Benkovci because there is another village named Polace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Polace near Sivo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see any heavy weapons there, the tanks or whatever it was that you mentioned, rockets, none of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the portion that talks about Mr. Zeljko Tisma and Orkans being fired on Muc and Split from the Polace area, do you recall the sound of outgoing rocket fire from the village of Polace?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You said you were mobilized several times. Where were you deployed to?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was deployed to Knin and also Kosovo. That's where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you referred to Kosovo, are you referring to a village close to Knin?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that village, the village of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We also saw in this statement where Mr. Despanic talks about how he and his group surrendered in Polace on the 5th of August. You had already been gone by that point. Did you hear subsequently from anyone about with RSK soldiers being present in Polace on the 5th of August and surrendering to the HV on or about that time?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear any of it, nor do I know who Despanic was, nor did anyone actually surrendered. I don't know. Maybe someone did do that, but my problems were far greater when I arrived Serbia, the problems I had to think about, so I have to say I'm sorry for every person who was killed or who suffered, whether Croat or Serb, but at the time when I was in Serbia, I had so many problems that I couldn't think about others. I just had to fight for the survival for my own family and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkovic, did you hear subsequently the fact that there were ARSK soldiers, such as Mjilkovic Mirko who refused to surrender and escaped to the nearby forest in the Polace area?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. As I already said, I didn't have the time nor the wish to listen to stories about who did what and how. So when you -- if you were in my position, had you arrived in Serbia without anything, I wonder whether you would be thinking about what to do to feed your family or about whether somebody had surrendered to someone or not. In other words, I was absolutely not interested in those kinds of stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Not having been present in Polace from the 5th of August onwards, you don't know whether there were ARSK soldiers still in the Polace area who had still refused to surrender. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I was not there. I left on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you also don't know whether there were any remaining ARSK soldiers in Mirkovici from the 5th of August onwards that refused to surrender. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the woman who told me about these things, this woman who had survived as -- in Mirkovici, Smiljana Mirkovic of the people there, Smiljana Mirkovic, Jovo Mirkovic and Petar Mirkovic had remained. And Petar's son, Milan, he too stayed back. These were unarmed people and if you think that people like that could defend themselves, well, then, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about people like that. I'm talking about people like Mirkovic Mirko who were combatants and you don't know whether people such as Mjilkovic Mirko were in Mirkovici on the 5th of August and thereafter. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify whom you mean? Who is this Mirko Mirkovic? I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirko Milkovic I said.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I read you a portion from a statement saying that there was a group of ARSK soldiers, some of whom surrendered in Polace, others who refused to surrender and went into the forest in the Polace area. My question to you again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, is that an accurate description of what you just read? It was about surrender. One person who wanted to stay in the woods and wait and the other one going home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, there was one who went home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and one who stayed in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Escaped, sorry; yes, correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... only the one who went to the woods, from what I remember you reading said that he refused to surrender, whereas the other just said, I'll go home. Nothing about whether or not to surrender. I want accurate --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine I can read it back verbatim: "We all wanted to surrender except for Mjilkovic Mirko, aka Koca, who threatening us to be traitors, escapes to the nearby forest --" I'm sorry, I was correct, Your Honour. That's Mirko Mirkovic. The second man is -- while Vuckovic Momcilo to return to his house on Polace saying that he would wait there for the HV soldiers and surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, others did not want to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was one who went home and would surrender, ones that would arrive and there was only one who said, I will not surrender, you are traitors, I'll go to the woods. So it wasn't an accurate --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. We have one person who said he refused to surrender, one person who said he was going home, but we don't know whether he surrendered. My question to you again is, you have no knowledge of whether these two individuals or others were in the village of Mirkovici and had, as much 5 August, 1995, and thereafter, refused to surrender to the HV, correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man that you are calling Mirko Mjilkovic, I don't know of this man. He is not from Polace. The other man, Momcilo Vuckovic this is an older man I think he was born in 1930 something and why would he be in Mirkovici when his house was about 600 meters away from Mirkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkovic, the question simply was whether you had any personal knowledge of persons, such as the two persons mentioned, whether they would have been after you had left in Mirkovici on let's say, the 5th of August, whether you have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir. I don't know anything about that. I have never heard anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those who told you what had happened after you had left, including the events in relation to your mother, did they ever tell you anything about ARSK soldiers being present, or not being present, in Mirkovici, after you had left? Did anyone ever tell you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir. All they talked about was about the Croatian soldiers who arrived in Mirkovici on the 5th of August already, and I think on the 5th, or the 6th of August, they took Jovo Mirkovic with them to Vrlika and then to the Lora prison in Split and in Mirkovici at that point were my mother, Smiljana Mirkovic, and as for any other people or any members of the military, the Serbian army, I don't know. I've never heard anything about that. These people who came on the first days, they told, that's what Smiljana recounted, they told these people who stayed back just stay at home, feed your cattle, no one will touch you, and that's how it actually was in the beginning, and on the 12th, that is when the event took place. All I know about the whole story is this. I don't have any other knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkovic, turning your attention to paragraph 8 of your 2007 statement you mention that when you reached Banja Luka we saw representatives of our authorities in Krajina who had returned from negotiations in Geneva. Would you please describe who you met with, who else was present, what was the discussion about, and where this took place?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want me to tell you exactly where this happened, I don't really know what part of Banja Luka it was in. It was in Banja Luka. As for representative of the Serbian Krajina, I saw there the late Milan Babic, Lazo Matsura [phoen] they said that he had returned from Geneva, and also Milje Prijic of whom they also said that he returned from Geneva, where they were discussing the Z-4 Plan, and this plan was, according to what we ordinary folk knew, was the plan that was offered to the republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was this a big meeting with a lot of people from the --

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, meeting? It was not a meeting? These were just people who came to a field, an open field. It wasn't even a square. And I don't know how these men happened to be there. Maybe when their convoy was directed off the road. I think Mr. Matsura was looking for his wife, and he was asking the people in the convoy what was going on and then they asked what was happening, because they were saying we are just back from Geneva, and we were negotiating there. So this is what I'm telling you is what I saw and heard myself. This is what I saw then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were these individuals, these representatives of the authorities in Krajina, were they addressing all of the people in the field, or was this just something that you heard as these representatives were passing?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As they were passing, there was a group of people, I don't know, maybe a couple of thousand people, and maybe there were some other people like that who talked about it in some other places, but I don't know, I did not talk to them directly. Someone from our group asked, What are we going to do? And they said they didn't know. But no one had a microphone to address the people who were collected there. This was not a gathering or a rally. It was just a group of people and they were talking about this in this open space.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mirkovic, concerning the death of your mother, you didn't file any requests with the Croatian authorities until 2004 or 2005. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. When we arrived Belgrade, and when reported to the Red Cross, we first registered with the International Red Cross and then with the Red Cross of Yugoslavia, I think; and we registered there the members of our family who had left, who had arrived Serbia. My mother had stayed behind, at home. And then later on when I heard about my mother's death, then I reported to the same organisations that my mother had been killed. After this, I did not ask about or search for, I thought that somebody from these international organisation would do to that, but at this point, later on, much later, I went to Veritas in Belgrade and they told me that I can submit a request to the Croatian government for an exhumation of my mother's remains. That's when I did that, but up to this moment, nothing has been done. No follow-up, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I just need to confirm roughly the year that you filed that request. Am I correct to say it was 2004 or 2005? Your witness statement, I believe, says two and a half years - let me find it. Paragraph 11 of your 2007 statement you say: "I filed a request about two and a half years ago." Is it correct to say, then, that given that this statement was given in March of 2007, that your request was given sometime in late 2004?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't say exactly what month or what date it was, but you can find that in the organisation, the organisation for the missing people and victims of war. The name of this organisation is Veritas, and you can find this information as to when I filed this request there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Jovo and Smiljana Mirkovic also did not file any complaint with the Croatian authorities that your mother had been murdered. Is that accurate, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why would they file a complaint? Nobody filed anything. They were just neighbours, and they told me what had happened to my mother. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Given that your mother was buried by Jovo, do you know prior to the filing of your request in late 2004 whether there had been any notice to the Croatian authorities of the allegation that your mother had been murdered?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is not an alleged murder; it was a murder. And as for whether they were informed or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to your request for exhumation, who did you file that with?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said this. To Veritas in Belgrade. And they forwarded this to an organisation in Croatia that was supposed to forward it on. And according to these representatives in Belgrade, they -- there was no information, no new information on this, that nothing had been done in Croatia yet, that it was not something they were dealing with at that point yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the organisation in Croatia to whom Veritas was supposed to forward this?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever get a receipt or a confirmation letter or any other confirmation from any institution in Croatia that they had received your request for exhumation?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I never received anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ask the Office of the Prosecutor to see what they could do to conduct an exhumation?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were at my place and when we discussed this, that was one of the things that we talked about as well, and I thought that this whole procedure would be speeded up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One minute, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mirkovic. Your Honour, have I nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On behalf of General Markac's Defence, I will pose a few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you please when answering my question, pause before you actually begin so that the interpreters can interpret this into English and French.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkovic, could you please tell me what schools did you attend?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed the middle school for catering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you work, if you did work, after you finished school?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while, I worked at -- on the island of Ugljan for Zelena Punta [phoen] company and also on the island of Hvar, the hotel, a Hvar company. And after that I worked in Knin. I think since 1981 I worked in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you do, what kind of work?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked as a waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what schools did your wife finish?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She completed high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And your mother?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a housewife. She did not attend school -- actually, she did finish elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkovic you told us that you served in the army and that you were a cook in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of military duties did you have in the army of Republic of Serbian Krajina when you were mobilized?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone did or had assignments according to the military speciality that they had in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did I understand your answer correctly you were a cook also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, one second. One second. Could you please put again the last question to the witness and ask him to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will need to repeat what you have said for interpretation. So my question was, did I understand you correctly that you also worked as a cook during the mobilisation for the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you issued any weapon?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was issued a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where was your weapon after -- once you were drafted?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where was your weapon kept when you were not mobilized?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the unit where I was assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What unit was this and where was its command?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its command was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkovic, please tell us -- my colleague has just reminded me that you did not reply when I asked you what unit you were serving in.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the name of the unit. I was just in the army. I don't know what you mean when you ask me about the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, so many years have passed. I really can't recall the name anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sir, how many able-bodied men with military training were there in the Polace area in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how many people lived there over all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe a ballpark figure then?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should do some clarification in order to do that for you. I simply never pondered the issue. I'm here to something else. The thought never crossed my mind that I would be asked questions about this. You see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps have any friends nearby, near your hamlet in the Polace area?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I had friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about those friends. Were they mobilized like you by the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were and some weren't. Some were fit for military service, and some weren't. Some dodged it. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that, on the 31st of July, 1995 President Milan Martic declared a state of war and general mobilization throughout the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him declaring a state of war. There was a war on and what that meant for us is we couldn't leave the homes, we had nothing to eat or drink, we weren't worrying about him declaring a state of war or anything. But I never heard and that must be the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup of the population in your area of residence?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my case, that was Polace. The population was entirely orthodox. Over in Knin, 92 per cent Serbs, the rest Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you talk about these figures or statistics, which period of time do you have in mind? Is that before the hostilities broke out in the area or do you mean after the Republic of Serbian Krajina was established?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time of the former Yugoslavia before it broke up in Knin. There were over 92 per cent Serbs that's what my information suggests. Perhaps you have other sources. Polace was always 100 percent orthodox. There were no Catholics or Muslims there. No Jews, no one else apart from Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are aware of what became of the Catholic population the Croats after the Republic of Serbian Krajina was established in the area?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard stories about people leaving some people staying behind, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at your 2007 statement. This is it P723, specifically paragraph 5 of your statement as well as paragraph 7 of your statement. You talk about the fact that your wife started crying when the war broke out, and she said that the Ustasha would kill all of you. This is followed in paragraph 7 by the following. You claim that your mother as well said that the Ustashas might as well kill her if they so wished? Mr. Mirkovic, in your family, was it usual for Croats to be referred to as Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't about Croats, generically speaking, it was about the soldiers milling around our area. They called our soldiers Chetniks and we called theirs Ustashas. That's how both parties referred to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is a derogatory term and a term that was used by your wife and by your mother who was no soldier, nor was she moving around any soldiers, as far as I understand?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 7 of your statement, your 2007 statement. You go on to state this. You say you weren't certain if you would be able to leave the Krajina area because you were a man. Can you please elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for that very reason. I wasn't certain that they would allow any men to leave the area. That's what I was thinking about. When I headed away from home, I was thinking would any of us men be allowed to leave the Krajina, and that's why I told my mother that she should leave with other ladies and other children. When I joined the column, I realized that there was no one checking on anyone else and I saw that this was the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkovic you told us a while ago that you had not been mobilized.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was. I would be on an on-and-off basis. Sometime I was and sometimes I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I could just complete my question before you start answering, I would be very grateful for that concession.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, if you introduce a question by stating the testimony of the witness which he finds inaccurate, incorrect, then the witness can interrupt you, Mr. Mikulicic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Mirkovic, my question, given what you told us a while ago, that at the start of Operation Storm, the 4th of August, 1995, you were not in fact mobilized, why, then, did you believe that men and you as a man would not be allowed to leave the territory of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know what thoughts were crossing other people's minds. Someone might have walked up to me and said, You're an able-bodied man, you are now mobilized, you have to stay. All I was thinking about at the time was to -- how to survive this horrible situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 you say some friends told you about the villages around Knin and about teams or groups of persons arriving in these villages telling the local population to pack and evacuate. Did they specify which groups of persons these were that were arriving in these villages?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No names were named, but probably those were people belonging to some local authorities. Like the civil protection or such-like. Probably. They told them to leave. They told them they had to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then, based on your statement, that evening you joined a convoy through Knin.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How were you travelling, you and your family?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had our own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you get your fuel?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult to come by fuel in that area. There was a lot of fuel being used up we had some coupons used every month. I'm not sure if that was on a monthly basis or not. Every month, each of us were entitled to a total of 20 litres of fuel and we could get some oil as well to work our land. I saved mine up in order to stop myself from using it all up at once and then I had some still remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far would that take you, a full tank?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took me as far as Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about after that?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, there was some petrol stations. They had fuel and everybody was free to go and get some.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain this. This is something you state in paragraph 8. You say that there would be no turning back that there would be no returning to Krajina and that was after you joined that convoy.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this long convoy leaving. All these people leaving, no one stopping them. At no point along the road, no one was telling them, Don't go. Stay. I realized then there would be no turning back and that there would be no staying in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say that you were receiving coupons for fuel. Can you please describe the procedure briefly how was this organised and who gave these coupons to you, how were they distributed?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those of us who had a vehicle that was registered in an orderly American that went there applied and we each got 20 litres of fuel a month, give or take a fuel. Sometime there is was enough to go around and sometimes not and when I say we got it, I don't mean for nothing. We bought this fuel. And we used these coupons in order to buy fuel from these people. We didn't just get it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. There was a way to make it possible for you to buy some fuel. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, you still didn't answer my question. Who did you get the coupons from, who distributed them which specific institution or organisation?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was the same body that we registered our vehicles with. I'm not sure what it is called it was the SUP, the S-U-P, the police, in other words that was where you would go with your vehicle registration papers and you would then be issued a coupon that was worth 20 litres of fuel and that was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the Chamber unanimously is wondering what is the point. Would you either come to your point or move to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that there was a depo at Polace where fuel was being kept for the eventuality of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there is no depot there, there is no petrol station this is just not true there was no place to keep fuel there. Where does one keep fuel? At petrol stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A while ago, you mentioned the Geneva talks and the Z-4 plan. Do you know about the fact that the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, specifically Milan Martic, refused this plan that provided for the autonomy of the Republic of Serbian Krajina within Croatia simply by dropping the issue all together even before the talks started and the map was discussed?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information about this was the information that I received as an ordinary citizen I knew this was a plan that was being considered but I didn't know specifics. I heard bits of this and bits of that what should have been done and would be done, but simply I wasn't privy to any detail. Just as I didn't read that book by that general wrote therefore you can hardly expect me to say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 11 of your statement dated 2007. This is the exhumation request. This is what you said there. You say that you had heard from some neighbours who had previously return to the village about them seeing civilian police around the place. First of all, Mr. Mirkovic, I'm ever so slightly confused because a minute ago you told my friend Mr. Misetic that no one remained in the village and now you're telling us that you talked to some neighbours who returned to the village. So what does this mean then? Was there anyone living in the village or not?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Mirkovici. I'm talking about general Polace area and indeed there were people who eventually returned to the general Polace area. Elderly people who simply went back to die.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I continue? You're telling us about your neighbours seeing civilian police around, that location. I suppose by location you mean Mirkovici, right?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The exact location where the remains of my mother were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the specific people who shared this information with you?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not? Dragoljub Tadorovic, who said that they had been to see him, policeman wearing plain clothes and they also asked about my whereabouts and they also asked him if he knew the whereabouts of my mother's burial site or grave; and he took them to the very spot and pointed it out to them. This man then said -- we know everything we know exactly who killed her. This shouldn't be a problem. I'm just telling you what that man told me. This is hearsay. I didn't hear this myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I do realize that, but I don't quite realize who said what.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policeman wearing civilian clothes, are you listening to me? I'm talking about the policeman who went there and he went to Dragoljub Tadorovic and wanted him to show where we had lived and he wanted to see where my mother had been buried and then this policeman said, We know exactly who killed her. There shouldn't be a problem with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Having heard this, did you maybe go back to the police to see if you could find out more about their information. You were at one point told about the police knowing who the perpetrator of the crime against your mother was?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which police are you talking about, sir, if you don't mind me asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I assume Croatian police in your village?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Croatia's police but whose police should I go to and ask these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe we're just talking at cross purposes here, Mr. Mirkovic. It is my duty to ask you questions. If you know the answers, please state them.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but I was in no position to talk to Croatian police. I simply wasn't able to do that. I never returned to Polace after 1995 and I am not here to name any names, who killed my mother. I know someone did. I don't know who. I don't want to go too far and name some person or another. I'm not here to lay the blame at anyone's door. What I'm here to say is the truth. My mother was murdered. I'm not here to blame, I'm not here to point my finger or indeed to defend anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand that and I respect that.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that you were in touch with Mr. Savo Strbac from Veritas, did you perhaps try to enlist the assistance of that organisation in order to see what results, if any, the Croatian police investigation had achieved about these events?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked to know who it was that killed my mother. All I asked for was to have a chance to bury my mother's mortal remains in a dignified manner and take her to our family grave. I never wanted to know who exactly killed my mother. I don't think I want to know. One thing I do know is it was no human being it was a beast who killed an old lady, aged 70. No human being in their right state of mind could possibly have done that. Serb or Croat. I'm trying to see this matter from a more generically humane position, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkovic, have no doubt about this, please, that's what we're all trying to do here, to see in a more humane perspective. My last question: How exactly did you get in touch with Mr. Strbac for Veritas?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the -- caught wind of the existence of this organisation and then I went straight to them to report my case that was in Belgrade. I think roughly about the same time there people who came over from some international organisation they took blood samples from me and my sister in order do some DNA analysis. I heard about the organisation and thought I would go straight to them and speak to them about this. I didn't know who else to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Strbac go back to some previous period when he was a secretary of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'd heard his name being mentioned on TV, that sort of thing. They were talking about human suffering about searches for missing persons and victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: SAVA MIRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Waespi, any further need to put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bench has no further questions for you either, Mr. Mirkovic. This concludes your testimony in this court. The Chamber is aware that the events you have testified about are about, as you told us, the loss of your mother. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to testify and to answer the questions that were put to you by the parties and by this Bench, and we wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for calling me. My greetings and my very best wishes to you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Mikulicic, the witness said that he was not -- he said he never returned to Polace, and he said: I never wanted to know who exactly killed my mother. I'm trying to see this matter from a more generically humane position. That means overview rather than what actually and precisely happened. You then said, Mr. Mirkovic, have no doubt about this, please, that's what we are all trying to do here, to see in a more humane perspective. Where the witness made a distinction between knowing about the facts and a more generically approach generically human approach, where you referred to all, I have to bring to your attention that this Chamber, of course, is trying to seek as much concrete information, not to say that the generic humane approach would not be of interest but certainly not to replace our wish to receive as much evidence on the facts and all the details available. I just wanted to put this on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- aware of it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as scheduling is concerned from what I now understand, Mr. Waespi, that there's no chance that the witness who was next scheduled not only would not appear today, but there is no chance that that witness will appear tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This means that the next witness we'll hear testimony of will be on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is correct. There is one option to move the videolink forward to Thursday afternoon and all party, including Mr. Monkhouse who did a great effort to reorganize, we could start around 3.00 on Thursday afternoon. I'm not sure whether that helps us a lot but these are the two options we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is there a fair chance that we would then finish the videolink evidence, because, for other reasons, having some additional time on Friday would not be bad. If we would start at 3.00 that would mean that we have a session of effective three hours would that do for the videolink witness? A little bit over three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sure that the Prosecution will not -- we are scheduled for 1.5 hours but I'm confident that Mr. Hedaraly who will lead the witness will not take more than one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my question to the Defence is for the videolink witness, if the Prosecution would take one hour would, it be possible to conclude the testimony of that witness on that same day, because as you will understand I have great difficulties in accepting that we would have to send the witness home and then to have her return again on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that, Your Honour, I will be the first one to examine the witness on behalf of Markac Defence and I don't estimate it to take more than one and a half hour. I will try even to squeeze this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes that. Would make so two and a half hours. Could I get an impression from other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of the Gotovina Defence, obviously we have to see what happens, but at this point we would have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no scheduled questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let me confer for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although the schedule for preparations will be rather tight, there seems to be a fair chance that the witness could commence giving evidence at approximately 3.00 on Thursday, in the afternoon, and that of course doesn't change anything, because I do understand that the witness next to that might be available on Friday, but that Defence counsel have strongly opposed against hearing the evidence of that witness. Now, is that a witness, Mr. Waespi, how much time would the then next witness take in chief, because preparing for cross-examination, of course is a different matter from hearing the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: According to -- this is Witness 98. According to the 65 ter estimate it is 2.5 hours, but I'm sure this could be reduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think as a matter of fact that that is exactly what the Defence opposes against that they would have to start the cross-examination on Friday. If cross-examination would start on next week --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour that would be beneficial for me, Your Honour, because I cannot be here on Friday and that is my witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. Would there be any problem with the Defence teams if the witness would give his evidence in-chief on Friday, so that we could start immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with the cross-examination on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I really have a difficulty with that because I'm not going to be here, and I don't want to have to read his transcript to prepare for cross-examination which is what I would have to do. I was all prepared for him to be examined as is scheduled on Monday and understanding the difficulties that have occurred recently that are not a problem of the Prosecution, it's just you know that happened. Things happened sometimes. My preference is keep this particular witness on Monday, the direct, because it is my witness. I have been preparing for that witness and would really rather be here but I can't be because I have a conflict on Friday, will be gone, out of Holland on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll consider that. Let's at least, for several reasons, let's reschedule the videolink witness for Thursday in the afternoon, with the firm expectation that the Defence team would not take any longer than Thursday afternoon, based on the assumption that we would not start later than 3.00. We would further consider whether we would start on Friday. Mr. Waespi, please assist me. The witness to follow the video conference witness, was he firmly scheduled to start at Monday only, or was he scheduled to follow the video-conference witness. Of course, I'm considering this, Mr. Kuzmanovic, you will understand to what extent the Chamber will have to consider your absence because if that witness would have been scheduled just as a follow-up witness to the videolink witness then of course it might be different compared to a situation where it was firmly scheduled that the follow-up witness would not start his examination-in-chief this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think I would put him into the category of being firmly scheduled for Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's at least then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that we have the witness order that we received from Mr. Waespi and that's what it showed. Your Honour, just so you know I have to serve on a jury in my home state, so I deferred it twice and I can't defer it a third time so I'm leaving tomorrow and I will be back on Monday, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Serving justice in a different capacity, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Yes. That's one thing. That's for Thursday. For tomorrow, I would like to go with the parties through the MFI list and how much time that takes depends on all of us. And we'll have no further programme then on Wednesday in the afternoon apart perhaps from some other housekeeping matters. Then since we have not that much time left, I would like to deliver one oral decision at this moment before we adjourn. This is a decision on the admission into evidence of a document, marked for identification, P320. On the 29th of May of this year, at transcript page 3933, the chamber admitted into evidence an UN report as P318. On the same day, at transcript page 3997, the Prosecution tendered into evidence under seal the annexes to the report, which were marked for identification as P320 on the grounds that it simply reproduced third-party information which the Defence was not in a position to challenge. The -- I am afraid that I missed one line. I'll start reading again, where I said that the Chamber admitted into evidence a UN report as P318. On the same day, at transcript page 3997, the Prosecution tendered into evidence under seal the annexes to the report, which were marked for identification as P320. And that's where I made my mistake. On the 11th of June, 2008, the Defence objected to the admission of P320 on the grounds that it simply reproduced third-party information, which the Defence was not in a position to challenge. The Prosecution responded that the arguments of the Defence should go to weight rather than admissibility. The Defence objections and Prosecution response can be found at transcript pages 4830 to 4833. Under Rule 89 (C), the Chamber may admit into evidence any exhibit that is relevant and probative. P320 contains one incident report, several clearly sourced statements taken by UN staff an associated photos. The statements were not taken for the purpose of proceedings before this Tribunal, and therefore do not fall within the scope of Rule 92 bis. The documents are contemporaneous, concern incidents reported to have taken place in the former UN Sector South during or after Operation Storm and are relevant and probative to allegations made in the indictment. Furthermore, they clarify the sources of the UN report admitted as P318 and enhance the Chamber's ability to properly assess the weight to be given to that report. The Chamber therefore admits P320 into evidence, under seal. The Chamber will take into consideration the arguments raised by the Defence when ultimately assessing the weight to be attributed to P320. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission of P320. Then, I think, this is an decision still missing on the admission of D723 and D724 which were this afternoon tendered by you, Mr. Misetic. There were no objections against these two documents. Therefore, D723 and D724 are admitted into evidence. We adjourn until tomorrow, Wednesday, the 27th of August, quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom.
